Downstream analysis I: genes differentially expressed along a ligand-receptor field trajectory

Kai Li

2026-10-15

  • Setup
  • Rebuild the field
  • The trajectory is the field itself
  • Fit the trajectory
  • Test genes along the trajectory
  • Visualise the trajectory genes
  • What the trajectory genes are

The previous tutorials stop at the field: they show how to estimate the ligand-receptor interaction as a spatial vector field, and how to score and visualise it. This one asks a transcriptional question:

Along the direction in which a ligand-receptor pair signals, which genes change their expression?

Answering it means treating a field quantity as a trajectory. Take one LR pair and look at its field potential U: every spot now sits at some position on the ligand-to-receptor axis, and gene expression can be modelled as a function of that position. We use tradeSeq to fit that function, which is why it is listed as a suggested dependency of spWAVE.

Setup

library(magrittr)
library(dplyr)

library(Seurat)
library(ggplot2)
library(spWAVE)

Rebuild the field

We reuse the 10x Visium mouse brain dataset and the small TGFb/FGF database from the first tutorial, so the field values here are the same ones. The field takes a few seconds; the trajectory fit below takes several minutes.

#** folder holding the tutorial dataset, adjust it to your local copy
data_dir <- "../../data"
brain <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, "mouse_brain_anno_clu.rds"))

mouse_db <-
  load_database(db_source = "CellChat", db_species = "mouse", filter_type = "Secreted")
#** a smaller subset, as in the field tutorials
mouse_db %<>% dplyr::filter(Family %in% c("TGFb", "FGF"))

brain_spWAVE <- create_spWAVE_object(brain, mouse_db, assay = "SCT")
brain_spWAVE <- brain_spWAVE %>% perform_LR_field_calc()

The trajectory is the field itself

Extracting one LR pair gives a data.frame with the field vector (Ex, Ey), the field potential (U), the ligand and receptor expression, and their difference.

fgf1 <- perform_field_extract(brain_spWAVE, "Fgf1.Fgfr1")
fgf1 %>% head
#>                           y        x            barcode            Ex
#> AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1 4607.621 6213.208 AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1  4.400470e-04

#> AAACATTTCCCGGATT-1 -8.194620e-06 -3.874040e-05 3.959761e-05  0.0075663212

U is what we will use as the trajectory: the question is which genes, in the space the field potential lays out, are expressed along the way that space is arranged – so U goes in as the trajectory variable. Two things are worth being explicit about:

  • it is not a lineage pseudotime. Nothing is inferred about cell state ordering; U is a spatial quantity, and cells with the same potential are simply “equally far” along the ligand-to-receptor direction. Every cell joins the same single trajectory, which is why the cell weights are all 1.
  • the sign has a direction. A ligand field contributes positively to the potential and the receptor field negatively, so genes going up along U are the ones tracking the ligand side of the interaction.

The column name is itself an argument: traj_arg accepts any column of this data.frame, so Ex, Ey or E_strength can be used the same way. Which of them to hand it is a question about how you read the field space – the direction of the field, or only how strong it is – rather than about the method.

Fit the trajectory

The fit is the expensive step of this tutorial, so the call is shown here rather than run. The chunk after it loads a result computed in advance.

brain_fgf1 <- run_LR_tradeSeq(
  seurat_obj = brain,
  database_result = brain_spWAVE,
  LR = "Fgf1.Fgfr1",
  kept_db = brain_spWAVE@kept_db,
  traj_arg = "U",
  nknots = 6,
  parallel = TRUE,
  paral_workers = 2
)

Two things decide the cost: the fit covers every gene of the assay, not only the ligand and the receptor, and paral_workers trades memory for time rather than being a free speedup.

#** the object the call above returns
brain_fgf1 <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, "fgf1_trade_res.rds"))

The returned list carries both the fitted model and the field_df it was built from; the second is not optional, because the plotting step below needs it.

Test genes along the trajectory

fgf1_test <- run_tradeSeq_gene_test(brain_fgf1$trade_res, method_use = "association")
fgf1_test %>% head
#>          waldStat df pvalue meanLogFC p.adj
#> Fth1    1576.4486  3      0 0.7324038     0
#> Nrgn    1434.3478  3      0 1.0059456     0
#> Camk2n1 1124.6110  3      0 0.3649443     0
#> Mbp     1081.8579  3      0 0.6851428     0
#> Camk2a  1000.0012  3      0 0.7276876     0
#> Fbxl16   921.3384  3      0 0.4378477     0

run_tradeSeq_gene_test wraps the two tradeSeq tests: "association" asks whether a gene’s expression changes at all along the trajectory, "startvsend" only asks whether the two ends of the trajectory differ. Both fill the genes whose GAM did not converge with neutral values instead of dropping them, and both report BH-adjusted p-values.

The test here is deliberately permissive – thousands of genes come back significant – because it tests a spatial gradient over a few thousand spots, not a designed contrast. Rank genes by waldStat, rather than reading the p-value column as a list of discoveries. The table comes back sorted by it, so the top of it is the ranking; we carry the first 200 genes into the figures below.

top_genes <- head(rownames(fgf1_test), 200)

Visualise the trajectory genes

ht_main <- plot_tradeTest_heatmap(
  brain_fgf1$trade_res,
  fgf1_test,
  brain_fgf1$field_df,
  select_genes = top_genes,
  n_split_row = 4,
  title = "Fgf1 -> Fgfr1 along the field potential"
)

Rows are genes, columns are positions along the trajectory, and the colour is expression after predictSmooth has evaluated each gene’s GAM at 100 points and each row has been scaled. So a row is not “expression in a cell” but “the shape of this gene’s response”. The Potential annotation bar underneath is the trajectory itself: mid grey is U = 0, blue is negative, red is positive. That is what makes the figure readable – a gene block that brightens towards the red end is induced on the ligand side.

The rows are split into n_split_row blocks (4 by default) by k-means on the response shapes, and that is where the biology shows up: with these 200 genes the two largest blocks – 75 and 62 genes – run in opposite directions, one rising towards the ligand side, one falling towards the receptor side. The rows carry no labels because 200 gene names do not fit; the two blocks are read back out of this figure below and drawn on their own, with their names shown.

select_genes takes any gene list, so the same call shows an arbitrary set of genes by name – it masks both top_n_gene and order_by. The two block figures below are drawn that way.

What the trajectory genes are

Each block is a group of genes with the same response shape, so the blocks are the natural unit to test. They do not have to be recovered by clustering again: the split is already in the figure, and row_order() reads the members of each block straight off it.

#** row_order() indexes the rows of the matrix the heatmap was drawn from, which is the
#** gene vector that was passed in -- so the block members are read off by position
block_genes <- ComplexHeatmap::row_order(ht_main) %>% lapply(function(i) top_genes[i])
lengths(block_genes)
#>  1  2  3  4 
#> 75  8 62 55

#** the two largest blocks, labelled by the direction their mean response runs in
yhat   <- tradeSeq::predictSmooth(brain_fgf1$trade_res, gene = top_genes, nPoints = 100, tidy = FALSE)
scaled <- t(scale(t(yhat)))
big <- names(sort(lengths(block_genes), decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]
rise <- sapply(big, function(b) { p <- colMeans(scaled[block_genes[[b]], , drop = FALSE]); p[100] - p[1] })
big <- big[order(-rise)]
names(big) <- ifelse(sort(rise, decreasing = TRUE) > 0, "rising (ligand side)", "falling (receptor side)")
names(big)
#> [1] "rising (ligand side)"    "falling (receptor side)"

The two blocks run in opposite directions, so each is worth looking at on its own. One figure per block, with the members of that block as select_genes and their names shown; the two are drawn side by side.

block_ht <- Map(function(genes, label)
  plot_tradeTest_heatmap(
    brain_fgf1$trade_res,
    fgf1_test,
    brain_fgf1$field_df,
    select_genes  = genes,
    show_rownames = TRUE,
    n_split_row   = 1,
    title         = paste0("Block: ", label)
  ),
  block_genes[big], names(big))

Then a plain over-representation test per block. The universe is the set of genes that were actually fitted, not the genome: a whole-genome background would report the expression filter as if it were enrichment.

library(clusterProfiler)
library(org.Mm.eg.db)   # Bioconductor mouse annotation

block_enrich <- lapply(big, function(b)
  enrichGO(block_genes[[b]], OrgDb = org.Mm.eg.db, keyType = "SYMBOL", ont = "BP",
           universe = rownames(fgf1_test), pAdjustMethod = "BH",
           pvalueCutoff = 0.05, qvalueCutoff = 0.2, readable = TRUE))
library(enrichplot)
#> enrichplot v1.26.6 Learn more at https://yulab-smu.top/contribution-knowledge-mining/
#> 
#> Please cite:
#> 
#> G Yu. Thirteen years of clusterProfiler. The Innovation. 2024,
#> 5(6):100722
library(patchwork)
wrap_plots(Map(function(eg, l) dotplot(eg, showCategory = 15) + ggtitle(l),
               block_enrich, names(big)), ncol = 2)

Each block comes back as one family and no term appears in both: the rising block is myelin and oligodendrocyte terms (ensheathment of neurons, myelination, oligodendrocyte differentiation), the falling block is synaptic terms (synapse organization, postsynaptic membrane potential, glutamate receptor signalling). U is a spatial axis, so a block that tracks it also tracks anatomy – here the positive end is hindbrain, the negative end hippocampus and cortex.
